items.answer: The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline contains five stages: first object representation, second modeling transformation, third lighting, fourth the viewing pipeline, and fifth scan conversion.

The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is the stage-wise process that computes the intensity values for each pixel, stores them in the frame buffer, and uses them to drive the display mechanism through the video controller.
The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline contains five stages: first object representation, second modeling transformation, third lighting, fourth the viewing pipeline, and fifth scan conversion.
The first stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, object representation, defines the objects that together form the rendered image in each object's own local coordinate system.
The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline contains five stages: first object representation, second modeling transformation, third lighting, fourth the viewing pipeline, and fifth scan conversion.

The second stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, modeling transformation, transforms objects from their local coordinate systems to the common world coordinate system to construct the scene.

questions.question: Why is some computer graphics knowledge needed to understand rendering?
options: Because rendering is covered by computer graphics
Because object representation determines the pixel intensities
Because rendering produces auditory stimuli for immersion
Because VR headsets use engineered lenses to guide light
questions.explanation: Rendering is covered by computer graphics, so knowledge of computer graphics is needed to understand the complexities involved in rendering.

questions.question: What makes rendering a key component of an immersive experience?
options: It augments the real environment with virtual content
It guides light from displays to the retina using lenses
It renders the scene in front of the user's eyes on the display device
It performs lighting in the world coordinate reference frame
questions.explanation: Rendering is a key component because the scene is rendered in front of the user's eyes on the display device.

questions.question: How is object representation characterized in the 3D graphics pipeline?
options: It is the lighting stage in the world coordinate reference frame
It is the stage that determines pixel intensities
It is scan conversion to screen coordinates
It is the first stage and does not involve pixel-intensity computation
questions.explanation: Object representation is called the first stage for simplicity, although there is no computation related to intensity calculation or pixel intensities.

data.text: Rendering is the key component of any immersive experience, so some knowledge of computer graphics is needed to understand the complexities involved. Object representation in the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is called the first stage for simplicity, although there is no computation as such related to intensity calculation or determination of the pixel intensities.
points: Knowledge of computer graphics is needed to understand the complexities involved in rendering.
Object representation is called the first stage of the 3D graphics pipeline for simplicity.

questions.question: Which stage of the 3D graphics pipeline transforms an object's local coordinate description into a world coordinate description?
options: Scan conversion
Modeling transformation
Lighting stage
Viewing pipeline
questions.explanation: Modeling transformation is the stage that transforms a local coordinate description to a world coordinate description.

questions.question: Which stage of the 3D graphics pipeline contains clipping and hidden surface removal in the 3D view coordinate system?
options: Scan conversion
Modeling transformation
Viewing pipeline
Lighting stage
questions.explanation: The viewing pipeline includes clipping in the 3D view coordinate system and hidden surface removal in the 3D view coordinate system.

data.text: The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline consists of five stages in order: object representation in the local coordinate system, modeling transformation, lighting, the viewing pipeline, and scan conversion. The viewing pipeline specifically contains viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.
points: The 3D graphics pipeline consists of five stages: object representation, modeling transformation, lighting, the viewing pipeline, and scan conversion.
The viewing pipeline includes viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.

questions.question: What is the purpose of modeling transformation?
options: To place an object's local-coordinate description into a world-coordinate scene
To determine the viewer's pose relative to an anchor in the real world
To measure an object's position using a magnetic field and receiver
To convert a world-coordinate scene into a device-coordinate description
questions.explanation: Modeling transformation applies operations to an object's local or object coordinate system description so the object can be placed in a common scene or world coordinate system.

questions.question: What is an object's local or object coordinate system description?
options: A common world-coordinate frame shared by all objects in a scene
A device-coordinate description of points after scan conversion
A screen-coordinate grid used to display rendered pixels
An individual definition of the object in its own coordinate reference frame
questions.explanation: A local or object coordinate system description defines an object's position and dimension in its own coordinate reference frame.

questions.question: Which operations are the basic transformations in modeling transformation?
options: Calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction
Lighting, projection, scan conversion, and pose estimation
Translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing
Translation, projection, clipping, and hidden surface removal
questions.explanation: The basic transformations in modeling transformation are translation, rotation around an axis, scaling, and shearing.

questions.question: Why are combinations of the basic transformations useful in modeling transformation?
options: They can determine the viewer's pose relative to an anchor
They can correct drift in an electromagnetic tracker
They can create any transformation required to construct a scene
They can convert device coordinates into screen pixels
questions.explanation: Combinations of translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing can create any transformation required to construct a scene.

data.text: Modeling transformation applies operations to an object's local coordinate system description to place it in a common world scene. An object's local coordinate system description defines its position and dimensions in its own reference frame. The basic transformations are translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing, and combinations of these four can create any transformation required to construct a scene.
points: Modeling transformation applies operations to an object's local coordinate system description to place it in a common world scene.
An object's local coordinate system description defines its position and dimensions in its own reference frame.
The basic transformations are translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing.

questions.question: Why are 2D transformations represented by 3×3 matrices and 3D transformations by 4×4 matrices in homogeneous coordinates?
options: Because one extra dimension is added to the coordinate system
Because the number of dimensions stays the same as in ordinary coordinates
Because two extra dimensions are added to the coordinate system
Because one dimension is removed from the coordinate system
questions.explanation: A homogeneous coordinate system adds one extra dimension, so 2D transformations use 3×3 matrices and 3D transformations use 4×4 matrices.

questions.question: Which 2D transformations in homogeneous coordinates are represented by 3×3 matrices?
options: Rotation, scaling, shearing, and clipping
Translation, rotation, scaling, and lighting
Translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing
Translation, scaling, shearing, and scan conversion
questions.explanation: 2D translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing can be represented by 3×3 matrices in homogeneous coordinates.

questions.question: How is a point in an object's local coordinate system transformed to the world coordinate system?
options: Represent it as a row vector P and multiply it by the transformation matrix S
Represent it as a column vector P and multiply it by the transformation matrix S
Represent it as a column vector P and add it to the transformation matrix S
Represent it as a column vector P and subtract it from the transformation matrix S
questions.explanation: The local point is represented as column vector P, and multiplying P by the transformation matrix S gives the transformed point P′.

questions.question: When each point on an object's surface is multiplied by the transformation matrix, what is the intended result?
options: New points that should be in the world coordinate system
New points that should be in the device coordinate system
New points that should be in the view coordinate system
New points that should be in the local coordinate system
questions.explanation: Multiplying the points on the object's surface by the transformation matrix produces new points that ideally are in the world coordinate system.

data.text: Transformations are typically represented by matrices in a homogeneous coordinate system where an extra dimension is added. Two-dimensional translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing can be represented by 3x3 matrices. A point in an object's local coordinate system is transformed to the world coordinate system by multiplying its column vector by the transformation matrix.
points: Transformations are typically represented by matrices in a homogeneous coordinate system where an extra dimension is added.
Two-dimensional translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing can be represented by 3x3 matrices.
A point in an object's local coordinate system can be transformed to the world coordinate system by multiplying its column vector by a transformation matrix.

questions.question: When is a composite transformation matrix used in constructing a world-coordinate scene?
options: When a point is first defined in the object’s local coordinate system.
When lighting models assign color to the object’s surface.
When more than one basic modeling transformation is needed to place an object.
When a single basic transformation is enough to place the object in the scene.
questions.explanation: A composite transformation matrix is used when constructing a world coordinate scene requires multiple basic transformations, such as translation, rotation, scaling, or shearing.

questions.question: In transforming rectangle ABCD into the chimney shape A′B′C′D′, what sequence of basic transformations is required?
options: Shearing is applied first, and scaling is applied second.
Translation is applied first, and scaling is applied second.
Rotation is applied first, and translation is applied second.
Scaling is applied first, and translation is applied second.
questions.explanation: The transformation cannot be done with one basic transformation; the example requires scaling first and then translation.

questions.question: In the transformation from rectangle ABCD to the chimney shape A′B′C′D′, what geometric change is represented by scaling with Sx = 0.5 and Sy = 1?
options: The rectangle is halved in length while its height remains unchanged.
The rectangle is doubled in length while its height remains unchanged.
The rectangle is doubled in both its length and height.
The rectangle is halved in both its length and height.
questions.explanation: Sx = 0.5 halves the object’s length, while Sy = 1 leaves its height unchanged.

questions.question: Why must the first applied transformation be placed rightmost when forming a composite transformation matrix?
options: Matrix multiplication is not commutative, so an incorrect sequence can produce an incorrect transformed result.
The first transformation is always translation, so its matrix must be placed rightmost.
The individual matrices are added together, so their order does not affect the transformed result.
Matrix multiplication is commutative, so the matrices can be arranged in any order without changing the result.
questions.explanation: Composite matrices are arranged right to left according to the order of application because matrix multiplication is not commutative; changing the sequence may change the result.

questions.question: How are the transformed vertices A′, B′, C′, and D′ obtained from the original vertices?
options: Each vertex is added to the composite transformation matrix.
Only the original vertex D is multiplied by the composite transformation matrix.
Each vertex is multiplied by the composite transformation matrix.
Each edge of the rectangle is multiplied by the composite transformation matrix.
questions.explanation: The transformed vertices are obtained as A′ = M A, B′ = M B, C′ = M C, and D′ = M D, where M is the composite transformation matrix.

data.text: A composite transformation matrix is used when multiple geometric or modeling transformations are required. These matrices are arranged from right to left based on the order of application because matrix multiplication is not commutative. Each current vertex is multiplied by the transformation matrix to obtain the transformed vertices.
points: Composite transformation matrices are used when multiple geometric or modeling transformations are required.
Matrices are arranged from right to left based on the order of application.
Transformed vertices are obtained by multiplying each current vertex by the transformation matrix.
The transformation sequence must be set correctly because matrix multiplication is not commutative.

questions.question: Which stage of the computer graphics pipeline assigns colors to objects in a scene?
options: Audio playback
Depth computation
Color computation
Object modeling
questions.explanation: The third stage is color computation, which uses lighting or shading models to assign colors to objects.

questions.question: Why are shading models used in computer graphics?
options: To reduce computation without compromising quality of experience
To eliminate the need for lighting models
To increase computation for more realistic colors
To map colors to continuous intensity values
questions.explanation: Shading models are used to reduce computation while maintaining quality of experience, while lighting models involve more computation.

questions.question: How are shading models related to lighting models?
options: Lighting models approximate and rely on shading models
They are more computationally intensive than lighting models
They approximate and rely on lighting models
They are identical in computation and result
questions.explanation: Shading models are approximations of the color-assignment methods used by lighting models, and they rely on lighting models.

questions.question: What values do lighting models use to compute colors?
options: Continuous normalized intensity values
Discrete transformation matrices
Continuous vertex coordinates
Discrete color values directly
questions.explanation: Lighting models compute colors as continuous intensity values, typically normalized, and then map them to discrete computer-supported values.

data.text: Color computation uses lighting or shading models to assign colors to objects for realistic perception. Shading models are approximations of lighting models used to reduce computation while maintaining quality. Lighting models compute continuous intensity values that are mapped to discrete values.
points: Color computation uses lighting or shading models to assign colors to objects for realistic perception.
Shading models are approximations of lighting models used to reduce computation while maintaining quality.
Lighting models compute continuous intensity values that are mapped to discrete values.

questions.question: When light from a source reaches a surface point and then reaches a viewer, what determines the color perceived by the viewer?
options: The medium through which the light travels
The intensity of the reflected light reaching the viewer's eye
The number of surrounding surfaces that reflect light
The intensity of the light emitted by the source alone
questions.explanation: The perceived color is determined by the intensity of the light that is reflected from the surface point and reaches the viewer's eye.

questions.question: In computer graphics, what is a lighting model used for?
options: To reduce computation by approximating the color assignment made by a lighting model
To define the sensors that measure a user's head position
To track a viewer's movement through a virtual environment
To simulate reflected light and compute the reflected-light intensity that represents a surface point's color
questions.explanation: A lighting model simulates the reflection of incident light from a surface point to the viewer's eye and computes the reflected-light intensity, which is essentially the surface point's color.

questions.question: How does the simple lighting model represent the total light intensity reaching a viewer from a surface point?
options: It selects the maximum of the ambient, diffuse, and specular intensities
It multiplies the ambient, diffuse, and specular intensities
It sums the ambient, diffuse, and specular intensities
It uses the photon, wave, and ray views of light
questions.explanation: The simple lighting model models the light intensity reaching the viewer as the sum of ambient, diffuse, and specular reflection intensities.

questions.question: Which statement correctly identifies the ambient, diffuse, and specular components of the simple lighting model?
options: Ambient comes from surrounding surfaces, diffuse is direct source light reflected diffusely, and specular is direct source light reflected with a shiny bright spot
Ambient comes from surrounding surfaces, diffuse is direct source light reflected with a shiny bright spot, and specular is direct source light reflected diffusely
Ambient is direct source light reflected diffusely, diffuse comes from surrounding surfaces, and specular is direct source light reflected with a shiny bright spot
Ambient comes directly from a source, diffuse is light reflected from surrounding surfaces, and specular is direct source light reflected diffusely
questions.explanation: The ambient component is light reflected from surrounding surfaces, the diffuse component is direct source light reflected diffusely, and the specular component is direct source light reflected with a shiny bright spot.

data.text: Perceived color is determined by the intensity of light reflected from a surface point to the viewer's eye. Computer graphics use lighting models to simulate this reflection and compute intensity. The simple lighting model represents intensity as the sum of ambient, diffuse, and specular components, where ambient light comes from surrounding surfaces and the other two components come from a light source.
points: Perceived color is determined by the intensity of light reflected from a surface point to the viewer's eye.
Computer graphics use lighting models to simulate this reflection and compute intensity.
The simple lighting model models intensity as the sum of ambient, diffuse, and specular components.
Ambient light comes from surrounding surfaces, while diffuse and specular components come from a light source.

questions.question: In the simple lighting model, what does a reflection coefficient value close to 1 represent?
options: A shiny, mirror-like surface where all incident light is reflected
A surface that receives no direct light from the light source
A surface that receives no ambient light from surrounding surfaces
A dull surface where most incident light is absorbed
questions.explanation: A reflection coefficient close to 1 represents a shiny, mirror-like surface where all light gets reflected, while a value close to 0 represents a dull surface with little reflection.

questions.question: How is the ambient component of reflected light intensity computed?
options: By multiplying the ambient light intensity at the point by Ks
By multiplying the ambient light intensity at the surface point by Ka
By multiplying the source light intensity by Ks
By multiplying the source light intensity by Kd
questions.explanation: The ambient component is computed by multiplying the ambient light intensity falling on the surface point by the ambient reflection coefficient Ka.

questions.question: When is the diffuse reflection component set to 0?
options: When N dot L is not greater than 0
When V dot r is not greater than 0
When Ka is not greater than 0
When the ambient light intensity at the point is 0
questions.explanation: The diffuse component uses the product of Kd, Is, and N dot L only when N dot L is greater than 0; otherwise it is set to 0, meaning no diffuse reflection.

questions.question: How is the specular reflection component computed when V dot r is positive?
options: As Ka times Is times (V dot L) raised to Ns
As Kd times Is times (N dot L) raised to Ns
As Ks times Is times (N dot L) raised to Ns
As Ks times Is times (V dot r) raised to Ns
questions.explanation: The specular component is the specular coefficient Ks multiplied by the source intensity Is and the dot product V dot r raised to the power Ns, provided V dot r is greater than 0.

questions.question: How is the ideal specular reflection direction vector r represented?
options: As 2(L dot N)N - L
As 2(V dot N)N - V
As V - 2(V dot N)N
As 2(N dot L)L - N
questions.explanation: The ideal specular reflection direction vector r is represented by twice the dot product of the light direction L and the surface normal N multiplied by N, minus L.

data.text: Reflection coefficients Ka, Kd, and Ks determine the fraction of incident light reflected from a surface based on its properties. The ambient component is computed by multiplying the ambient light intensity by Ka, while the diffuse component uses Kd, source light intensity, and the dot product of the surface normal and light direction. The specular component is computed using the Phong model, which relies on the Ks coefficient, source light intensity, and the dot product of the viewer direction and the ideal specular reflection direction.
points: Reflection coefficients Ka, Kd, and Ks determine the fraction of incident light reflected from a surface based on its properties.
The ambient component is computed by multiplying the ambient light intensity by the ambient reflection coefficient Ka.
The diffuse component is computed using the Kd coefficient, source light intensity, and the dot product of the surface normal and the light direction.

The specular component is computed using the Phong model, which involves the Ks coefficient, source light intensity, and the dot product of the viewer direction and the ideal specular reflection direction.

questions.question: In a lighting model, what form is the radial intensity attenuation factor typically computed in?
options: A constant factor determined by the spotlight angular limit theta
An inverse quadratic function of the distance d, using coefficients a0, a1, and a2
The cosine of phi raised to the positive exponent A1
An inverse linear function of the distance d, using coefficients a0, a1, and a2
questions.explanation: The radial intensity attenuation factor accounts for the diminishing of light intensity with distance and is typically computed as an inverse quadratic function of distance using coefficients a0, a1, and a2.

questions.question: Why is angular intensity attenuation included in a lighting model?
options: To create spotlight effects in which points inside the cone are bright and points outside are darker
To multiply the ambient light intensity by the ambient reflection coefficient
To calculate the ideal specular reflection direction from the normal and light vectors
To account for the reduction in light intensity as the distance from the source increases
questions.explanation: Angular intensity attenuation is considered primarily for generating spotlight effects, where elements inside the spotlight region are visible or brightly visible and elements outside the spotlight zone are darker.

questions.question: What values does the commonly used angular intensity attenuation factor take for a spotlight cone?
options: 0 outside the angular limit theta, and cos phi to the power A1 inside it
0 inside the angular limit theta, and cos phi to the power A1 outside it
A constant inside the angular limit theta, and 0 outside it
1 outside the angular limit theta, and an inverse quadratic function of d inside it
questions.explanation: The commonly used angular intensity attenuation factor is 0 when the surface point is outside the angular limit theta, and within that limit it varies as the cosine of phi raised to the power A1.

questions.question: In the modified simple lighting model, which intensity components are scaled by radial and angular attenuation factors?
options: The ambient component, with the diffuse and specular components unchanged
Only the diffuse component, with the ambient and specular components unchanged
The sum of the diffuse and specular components, with the ambient component unchanged
All three components: ambient, diffuse, and specular
questions.explanation: The I_M ambient component is left unchanged, while the sum of the diffuse component I_D and the specular component I_SPEC is multiplied by the radial and angular attenuation factors.

data.text: Intensity attenuation factors are needed because light intensity typically diminishes with distance from a source. Radial intensity attenuation typically uses an inverse quadratic function of the distance to model this diminishing light. Angular intensity attenuation is primarily used to generate spotlight effects, with factors varying based on whether a point is inside or outside a spotlight cone. In the modified model, these factors multiply the sum of the diffuse and specular reflection components while the I_M component remains unchanged.
points: Intensity attenuation factors are needed because light intensity typically diminishes with distance from a source.
Radial intensity attenuation typically uses an inverse quadratic function of the distance to model this diminishing light.
Angular intensity attenuation is primarily used to generate spotlight effects.
Angular attenuation factors are 0 outside a spotlight cone and vary as the cosine of the angle raised to a power inside it.
These factors multiply the sum of the diffuse and specular reflection components while the I_M component remains unchanged.

questions.question: In a colored light source model, how is the intensity of a light source represented?
options: As a four-element vector including an alpha channel
As a single scalar intensity value
As a three-element vector of red, green, and blue intensities
As a two-element vector of luminance and chrominance
questions.explanation: The model represents the emitted light intensity with three components corresponding to red, green, and blue, forming the vector Is = (Isr, Isg, Isb).

questions.question: What does a colored light source model do to the red, green, and blue parts of the source intensity?
options: Averages all color components into one monochrome intensity
Computes the combined color first and then splits it into components
Uses the red component alone to estimate the perceived color
Computes each color component individually and combines them to produce perceived color
questions.explanation: The red, green, and blue components are computed individually, and their combination gives the perception of any color.

questions.question: In a colored light source model, how are the reflection coefficients k, kd, and ks specified?
options: As two-element vectors for brightness and saturation
As single scalar values shared by all colors
As four-element vectors including a separate ambient term
As three-element vectors with a value for each red, green, and blue component
questions.explanation: The reflection coefficients are specified as three-element vectors, corresponding to the red, green, and blue components.

questions.question: How does a lighting model handle multiple light sources?
options: All source contributions are multiplied together and then added to the ambient intensity
Ambient intensity plus the sum of separately calculated source contributions, computed per RGB component
The source contributions are averaged once before being added to the ambient intensity
Only the brightest light source is used, and the others are ignored
questions.explanation: For n light sources, the model adds the ambient intensity to the summation of contributions from each light source, with each contribution calculated separately and, for colored sources, computed separately for red, green, and blue.

data.text: Colored light sources use red, green, and blue components that are computed individually to create any color. Reflection coefficients are specified as three-element vectors where each component has a value of one. The total light intensity is the sum of ambient light and the contributions from all light sources, with each contribution calculated separately for the red, green, and blue components.
points: Colored light sources have red, green, and blue components that are computed individually to produce any color.
Reflection coefficients are three-element vectors where each component has a value of one.
Total intensity is the sum of ambient light and the contributions from all light sources, calculated separately for each color.

questions.question: In intensity mapping, how do lighting-model intensities differ from device-supported intensities?
options: The model and display both support an infinite range, so no mapping is needed.
The model can produce any value from 0 to 1, while a display supports only a finite set of values.
The model produces only integer bit patterns, while a display can represent any real value from 0 to 1.
The display supports more intensity values than the lighting model can compute.
questions.explanation: A lighting model computes pixel intensities over an infinite 0-to-1 range, whereas a display has only a finite set of supportable intensity values.

questions.question: Why are successive device-supported intensity levels related by a multiplicative factor r?
options: Because humans perceive relative changes between intensity values rather than absolute changes in intensity.
Because the lighting model computes only absolute intensity values.
Because a display stores absolute bit patterns for each pixel.
Because a photometer can measure only absolute intensity values.
questions.explanation: The multiplicative factor reflects the psychophysiological property that perception is based on relative changes between intensities, not absolute intensity changes.

questions.question: What information is used to determine the device-supported intensity values?
options: The number of pixels, the minimum reflection coefficient Ka, and the maximum reflection coefficient Ks.
The source intensity vector Is, the colored reflection coefficient vectors, and the ambient intensity.
The distance d, the radial coefficients a0, a1, and a2, and the angular limit theta.
The number of levels n, the measured minimum intensity I0, and the known maximum intensity value 1.
questions.explanation: Device-supported values are determined from the number of levels, the photometer-measured minimum intensity I0, and the known maximum intensity value 1.

questions.question: How is a lighting-model pixel intensity stored for display?
options: It is mapped to the next higher table intensity, and that bit pattern is stored in the frame buffer at the pixel location.
It is mapped to the nearest table intensity, and the corresponding bit pattern is stored in the frame buffer at the pixel location.
It is mapped to the next lower table intensity, and that bit pattern is stored in the frame buffer at the pixel location.
It is stored in the frame buffer at the pixel location as the unmodified model intensity.
questions.explanation: A table stores the device-supported intensities and their bit patterns; the model intensity is mapped to the nearest table intensity and its bit pattern is written to the frame buffer.

questions.question: How is the multiplicative factor r for the device-supported intensity levels found?
options: By taking the average of the minimum intensity I0 and the maximum intensity value.
By using the relation In = r^n I0 with the known maximum intensity value.
By measuring each intermediate intensity value with a photometer.
By using the reflection coefficients of the simple lighting model.
questions.explanation: Successive levels are I1 = r I0, I2 = r^2 I0, and so on up to In = r^n I0, so r is obtained from that relation using the maximum intensity.

data.text: Lighting models produce an infinite range of intensities, but displays support only a finite set of values determined by the number of levels, minimum intensity, and maximum intensity. Successive device-supported values are calculated using a multiplicative factor because humans perceive relative changes in intensity. Lighting intensities are then mapped to the nearest supported value in a table to store the corresponding bit pattern in the frame buffer.
points: Lighting models produce an infinite range of intensities, but displays support only a finite set of values.
Device-supported intensity values are determined by the number of levels, the minimum intensity value, and the maximum intensity value.
Successive intensity values are calculated using a multiplicative factor because humans perceive relative changes in intensity.
Lighting intensities are mapped to the nearest supported value in a table to store the corresponding bit pattern in the frame buffer.

questions.question: How does modeling transformation connect object representation with lighting in the three-dimensional graphics pipeline?
questions.reference_answer: Object representation defines the objects that form the rendered image in each object's own local coordinate system. Modeling transformation then maps those local descriptions into a common world coordinate system so multiple objects can be assembled into a scene. Because lighting takes place in the world coordinate reference frame, it can use the assembled scene after modeling transformation.

questions.question: Why is the right-to-left order of transformation matrices important when forming a composite transformation matrix?
questions.reference_answer: A composite transformation matrix is used when constructing a world coordinate scene requires multiple basic transformations. It is formed by arranging the individual transformation matrices from right to left according to the order of application: the first transformation applied is placed rightmost, and subsequent transformations are placed to its left. Matrix multiplication is not commutative, so an incorrect sequence may produce an incorrect transformed result.

questions.question: How are lighting models related to shading models, and why can shading be useful in a graphics rendering pipeline?
questions.reference_answer: In the computer graphics pipeline, color computation uses lighting or shading models to assign colors to objects in the scene. If a color is not assigned, depth cannot be perceived and the quality of experience is reduced. Shading models are approximations of the color-assignment methods used by lighting models and involve less computation, so they can reduce computation without compromising the quality of experience.

questions.question: Why does intensity mapping need device-supported intensity levels when a lighting model has already produced pixel intensities?
questions.reference_answer: A lighting model can compute a pixel intensity as any continuous value between 0 and 1, but a display such as an 8-bit display supports only a finite set of intensity values, such as 256 values per pixel. Device-supported intensity values are determined from the number of levels, the minimum device-supported intensity value, and the known maximum value, using a multiplicative factor based on the psychophysiological property that humans perceive relative changes rather than absolute changes. A table stores these device-supported intensity values and their bit patterns, so the continuous pixel intensity is mapped to the nearest table intensity and the corresponding bit pattern is stored in the frame buffer.
